title: AI Isn't The Problem. Your Decisions Are.
author: By Title Only
source: The Best Leadership Newsletter on Substack, December 8, 2025
summary: The author builds the argument off the Iceberg of Ignorance: senior leadership, on average, knows 4% of a company's operational problems, while frontline workers know 100%. That gap matters now because senior leaders are the ones demanding AI integration without seeing the problems AI is supposedly there to solve. The framing of the piece is deliberately flip, but the point is serious. Companies are adopting AI as a solution before anyone has defined the problem. The visible symptom is tool-first thinking: AI picked because it makes you look innovative, scares competitors, and looks great in board decks. The middle of the piece is a usefully concrete five-pitfall taxonomy for the problem of starting at the solution. Teams automate the wrong thing. They create more work instead of less. They break processes that were not broken. They confuse and overwhelm employees. They waste money and morale. The one-line compression is that automating chaos produces more chaos. A worked example follows: a SaaS company with high-eight-figure revenue, seventy employees, and significant tech debt rerouted its roadmap to ship an AI product in six weeks because competitors had one. They lost three clients on broken promises, the AI product performed inconsistently on top of unresolved tech debt, and the clients that tried it asked for it to be removed. The corrective is a three-question litmus test to apply before authorising an AI initiative. What human pain are we trying to solve. What would success look like without AI. Is AI the simplest and most effective way to solve this, or is it just the coolest. If you cannot answer all three, you are not solving a problem, you are creating one. The piece closes on a second short story: a web-hosting company the author loved because its support team was human, authentic, and problem-solving. Three months before publication they replaced the team with AI, and service collapsed. They used AI to solve a problem they did not have. The generalisable line is that the future belongs to companies that adopt AI wisest, not fastest. Start with the problem, end with the tool.
points: The central argument of this piece is grounded in the author's engagement with how real people think and act, not in idealized or abstract reasoning.
The takeaway is actionable,it can be implemented at the classroom or school level without waiting for policy change or external resources.
The piece challenges a common default assumption in education practice and offers a concrete alternative framed by evidence or lived experience.
The stakes are clear: what happens if leaders or teachers adopt this approach, and what is the cost of continuing the current default.
quotes: There’s a thing called the Iceberg of Ignorance. It says that senior leadership only knows 4% of a company’s problems. Frontline workers know 100% of them. Yet it’s these same senior leaders who are making the big strategic decisions for companies, despite the fact they only know 4% of the problems.

Company leaders are treating AI as a solution, even though nobody has defined the problem. AI has become the corporate version of the flashy red Mustang in a mid-life crisis. But adding AI because “everyone else is doing it” is not innovation, that’s more like Halloween. Just because you’re dressed as a superhero, doesn’t mean you will fly.

When a company starts with the solution instead of the problem, there are five predictable pitfalls: They automate the wrong thing. They create more work instead of less. They break processes that weren’t broken. They confuse and overwhelm employees. They waste money and morale. Simply put, if you automate chaos, all you’re gonna end up with is more chaos.

Real problems have four specific characteristics: Pain: People are feeling pain (it’s not just execs with FOMO). Cost: You can measure the real cost of not implementing a solution. Problem: The people impacted by the problem can describe it in one sentence. Improvement: Solving the problem will quickly improve efficiency, revenue and sanity.
Our customer support team is drowning in tickets” is a real problem that needs fixing. “Our competitors are moving faster with AI” is not.

They abandoned their roadmap, rerouted resources, and built an AI product in six weeks. They lost three clients because they failed to deliver on promises. Because they ignored fixing the tech debt, the AI performs inconsistently, at best. The clients that tried it don’t understand why they need it and asked for it to be removed. Team morale has sunk lower than low.

If you think you’re putting the solution before the problem, here is a simple 3-question framework to keep you in check. What human pain are we trying to solve? What would success look like without AI? Is AI the simplest and most effective way to solve this, or is it just the coolest? If you can’t answer all three, you’re not solving a problem. You’re probably creating one.

The future doesn’t belong to the companies that adopt AI the fastest. It belongs to the companies that adopt AI the wisest. AI isn’t the threat. AI isn’t the enemy. AI isn’t coming for your job. Your poor decision-making is. So start with the problem. End with the tool.” Archived from The Best Leadership Newsletter on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
